video.title: Forget Storage Units. He Rents Out Empty Dirt Instead?!

summary: UpFlip host walks through Chris Conrad's 'Long Yards' business, which rents fenced, gated dirt lots (storage yards) to contractors and other tenants on month-to-month terms. Chris explains how he found tenants early on (approaching vehicles, flyers at Home Depot, online marketplaces), how land is evaluated (net rentable square footage, NOI, cap rate) and how deals can be done via purchase, lease or profit share with landowners using investor money. He claims one Canadian flagship nets $25k/month at a 62% margin and that he works about five hours a week with on-the-ground staff. The key takeaway is that the model is simple operationally but is really a land and real estate business that needs capital, partners and underwriting skill.

ideas.name: Contractor storage yards (Long Yards)
ideas.one_liner: Rent fenced, gated plots of dirt by the month to contractors and other businesses that need outdoor storage for vehicles, trailers and equipment.
ideas.business_model: Month-to-month rent per yard, sticky long-term tenants, with extra income from boxes and offices.
ideas.customer: Contractors, civil workers, tow truck and bus operators, car businesses, service businesses, and some homeowners with RVs or toys.
ideas.problem: Contractors and others cannot find secure, affordable outdoor storage for big equipment, trailers and fleets; supply is constrained.
ideas.offer: Gated, fenced yards of 1,000 to 5,000+ sq ft with power outlets, cameras, automatic gate lockout for non-payment, month-to-month flexibility.

pricing.model: Monthly rent per yard, varying by size and market
pricing.notes: Price is set by starting high and lowering until the lead-to-visit-to-close conversion rate hits target; tenants range from $25/month early on to $5-6k/month.

acquisition_channels.details: Early on Chris ran up to vehicles at red lights, approached tow truck drivers, and walked the Home Depot car park asking drivers with trucks if they need a storage yard; left flyers in door handles.

quote.text: I would literally run up to vehicles at a red light and be like, Hey, you need a storage yard.
quote.speaker: Chris Conrad

acquisition_channels.details: Posted on online marketplaces (Facebook Marketplace, Kijiji-style classifieds) to get the first few tenants.
Now spends roughly $500 to $1,000 a month; says Google, Facebook and listing sites perform best for ROI. Previously spent tens of thousands per month at some locations with poor results.
Classified and listing sites (transcript garbles names, e.g. 'classy and loop') produce leads.
Larger contractors now reach out directly; tenants are sticky and expand within the site.

ideas.delivery: Chris builds fenced yards on leased or owned land, with gates, power outlets and cameras. On-site staff (Eddie) keep sites clean and check security; an ops/sales assistant and a phone person handle enquiries and site visits. Tenants almost always visit before renting and are closed on site after qualifying questions (problem, solution, size, timing).
unit_economics_claims: Flagship Canada site nets $25k/month at 62% margin
US site: land about $1M, total about $3.5M, expected value $6.5M when leased up
Build-out payback on boxes about 1.5 to 2 years
Whiteboard example: 92,000 net rentable sq ft x $0.25 = about $23k/month, about $20k at 90% occupancy, about $16k NOI after $4k expenses
ideas.startup_cost: Very high for buy and build: about $3.5M for the US site and about $500k for another location. Lease route example about $350k total project with a 10% (about $35k) down payment. Chris says it can be done with investor or partner money.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Depends on build and permits; early yards were pre-sold to afford front gates, and the Canadian winter delayed things. Existing warehouse could be rented temporarily while permits take 3 months to 3 years.

acquisition.how: Inbound paid search, listings and SEO can be agent-run, but tenants insist on visiting in person and a human closes on site.

onboarding.how: Site tours, qualifying questions and on-site closing are human-led; only contracts and payment setup can be automated.

delivery.how: Requires physical land, fencing, build-out, permits, site cleanup and security by people on the ground.

billing.how: Recurring rent and automatic gate lockout for non-payment can be automated.

support.how: Phone enquiries (5 to 8 a day per site) and site issues are mostly handled by staff; some triage could be AI-assisted.

uk_applicability.notes: Concept (outdoor storage for vans, plant, trailers) exists, but SBA financing, US land and zoning economics are not transferable. UK needs planning permission/change of use for storage land, business rates, and land is scarce and costly. Landowner profit-share or lease approach could work with changes but needs large capital.

risks: Huge capital needs and real estate debt exposure
Chris himself filed a consumer proposal after earlier losses
Zoning, permits and wetlands/setbacks limit usable land
Land scarcity makes deals hard to find
Dependent on a single local market's demand and rates
Environmental issues such as fluids leaking onto land

ideas.name: Landowner partnership / lease or profit-share deal sourcing
ideas.one_liner: Find a suitable parcel, lock it up with a refundable deposit and due diligence, then bring investors and run a storage yard on a lease or profit share without owning the land.
ideas.business_model: Profit share or lease margin: pay the landowner a percentage or fixed rent (e.g. $6-8k/month) and keep the rest of the yard income.
ideas.customer: Landowners with suitable commercial land, plus investors/partners funding the build-out.
ideas.problem: Landowners have unused land but not the business model; aspiring operators have no capital.
ideas.offer: Operator brings the storage-yard model and manages it; landowner gets majority profit share or rent with no work.

pricing.model: Profit share (landowner gets majority) or fixed lease rent

price_points.label: example offer to landowner from about $20k/month income
10% down payment on the lease project

pricing.notes: SBA can finance up to 90% of the project; remaining 10% from partners.

acquisition_channels.details: Direct outreach to landowners and property owners; deal sourcing then locked by contract with a 90-day due diligence period and refundable deposit of about one month's rent.

ideas.delivery: Operator signs contract with landowner, does due diligence with the city, assembles investors and runs the yard business.
unit_economics_claims: Lease example: income about $20k/month, rent $6-8k/month, healthy margin and coverage ratio
Chris claims such a deal can produce $5-15k/month cash flow
ideas.startup_cost: About $35k down on a $350k lease project (10%), can be covered by partners; refundable deposit of about one month's rent to lock up.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated beyond 90-day due diligence plus build-out and permits.

acquisition.how: Landowner negotiation is relationship-driven; land search and screening could be tooled up.

onboarding.how: Contracts, investors and due diligence need human negotiation.

delivery.how: Same as the yard operation: physical build-out and site operations.

billing.how: Rent collection and landowner payouts can be automated.

support.how: Landowner and investor relationships require human attention.

uk_applicability.notes: Lease/profit-share structure works in principle in the UK but SBA is US-only; UK requires planning permission and legal leases, and funding must come from private investors or commercial lenders.

risks: Landowner may reject if terms are not competitive
Overestimating rent per sq ft makes the deal fail

quotes.text: You just need to find the deal. If you find a good deal, lock it up, lock it up and then put the deal together.
quotes.speaker: Chris Conrad

ideas.name: Container boxes and offices for yard tenants
ideas.one_liner: Add foldable storage boxes (Long Box) and site offices (Long Office) to yards to increase income per sq ft.
ideas.business_model: Monthly rental of boxes and offices alongside yard space.
ideas.customer: Yard tenants needing covered storage or office space, plus homeowners wanting sheds.
ideas.problem: Tenants need to keep some items out of the weather or need small office space.
ideas.offer: Folding boxes imported from Europe and offices rented month to month.

pricing.notes: Chris says payback is about 1.5 to 2 years.

acquisition_channels.details: Upsold to yard tenants and walk-in prospects who need a box or warehouse.

ideas.delivery: Boxes delivered and placed on site; physical assets.
unit_economics_claims: Box costs $2.5-3.5k, rents $150-300/month, payback 1.5 to 2 years

acquisition.how: Upsell to existing tenants; listing online.

delivery.how: Physical assets that need placement and maintenance.

uk_applicability.notes: Container/cabin rental is established in the UK, though planning rules for siting structures apply.

quotes.text: these come from Europe and they they fold the unfold, which is cool
quotes.speaker: Chris Conrad

ideas.name: Land bank play with storage yard income
ideas.one_liner: Buy premium land, put up a yard business quickly for income, and hold for appreciation as the city expands.
ideas.problem: Land held idle earns nothing while waiting for appreciation.
ideas.offer: Temporary storage-yard use generating cash flow while land value rises.
unit_economics_claims: US site bought for about $1M, total cost about $3.5M, projected value $6.5M when leased up

uk_applicability.notes: UK land is expensive and planning-constrained; the land-bank concept exists but needs heavy capital.

quotes.text: You could find premium land, pop this model up quickly and let it sit there until the city expands
quotes.speaker: UpFlip host

ideas.name: Self-storage / storage yard educational book and coaching
ideas.one_liner: Chris sells a book ('Sell Storage Yards: the Cash Flow Fast Pass') and teaches the model on YouTube.
ideas.problem: People do not know the asset class or how to underwrite it.
ideas.offer: Book and training on underwriting and deal sourcing.

acquisition_channels.details: Chris posts videos on YouTube and promotes his book there.

uk_applicability.notes: Education content sells anywhere, though content needs UK-specific numbers.

tactics.name: Cold approach for first tenants
steps: Go where people with trucks and trailers are (Home Depot car parks, red lights, tow truck drivers)
Ask 'Do you need a storage yard?' and target people who look like they can pull equipment
Leave flyers in vehicle door handles if they are not there
Also post on online marketplaces and be everywhere

quote.text: Excuse me, sure. Yeah, you mean, do you need a storage yard for any equipment?
quote.speaker: UpFlip host

tactics.name: Pre-sell yards to fund build-out
steps: Pre-sell yards by the year to tenants
Use the cash to afford front gates and fencing for the first five yards

quote.text: I had to pre-sell them by the year to afford the front gates to get it going.
quote.speaker: Chris Conrad

tactics.name: Price by conversion rate
steps: Price as high as you think the market will bear
Track leads, show-ups and closes as a sales pipeline
Lower price until conversion rate hits target

quote.text: we priced it as high as we thought we could. And then we let the market tell us.
quote.speaker: Chris Conrad

tactics.name: Underwrite land with net rentable sq ft
steps: Measure usable acres and convert to sq ft (3 acres = 130,680 sq ft)
Subtract about 30% for roads, wetlands and setbacks to get net rentable sq ft
Multiply by rate per sq ft (e.g. $0.25) and subtract about 10% vacancy
Deduct expenses (about $4k/month in example) to get NOI
Multiply NOI by 12 and divide by cap rate (8%) to find what the dirt is worth and what you can offer

quote.text: So now you got 92,000 net rentable square feet. So we need to figure out how much money you can make per square foot from this.
quote.speaker: UpFlip host

tactics.name: Lock up a deal with a refundable deposit
steps: Send a contract to the landowner with a 90-day due diligence period
Put down a refundable deposit of about one month's rent
Confirm zoning/permits with the city
Then assemble investors and funding

quote.text: Here's one month's deposit. I have 90 days of due diligence, which I need to confirm with the city
quote.speaker: Chris Conrad

tactics.name: Qualify tenants with a few questions
steps: Ask what problem they are solving, what size yard they need and when
Get them to visit the site and see security
Close on site when urgency is high

quote.text: Three, four pillar questions is all you need.
quote.speaker: Chris Conrad

tactics.name: Let demand set yard size mix
steps: Watch which sizes rent fastest and have the longest waitlist
Build more of those sizes
Use movable fencing so yard sizes can be reconfigured

quote.text: let the demand tell us and let's build this supply
quote.speaker: Chris Conrad

warnings.warning: Chris lost everything after a big box store did not pay his construction company, going from 14 employees to filing a consumer proposal.
Land is the real constraint: expensive, scarce and hard to get, so deals are hard to find.

quote.text: it's a land constraint business. So this isn't like farmland or residential land.
quote.speaker: Chris Conrad

warnings.warning: If rent per sq ft assumptions are wrong (e.g. 15 cents instead of 25 cents) the deal does not work, so validate market rates before approaching landowners or investors.
Spending tens of thousands per month on marketing did not work at some locations.
Don't trust people on words alone; inspect what you expect and use cameras and presence.

quote.text: don't trust people that word value. Like everyone like sounds good. But then you inspect what you expect
quote.speaker: Chris Conrad

warnings.warning: Permitting can take three months to three years, so plan interim use of existing buildings.

lessons.lesson: Learn the numbers (cost, value, income) before approaching landowners or investors, otherwise you are flying blind.

quote.text: So you got to know what it's worth, how much it's going to cost, and what it's going to make. Without that, you're flying blind.
quote.speaker: Chris Conrad

lessons.lesson: You can find the deal without owning the money: lock up a deal with a deposit and bring in partners.
Sticky, high-lifetime-value customers justify a higher CAC.

quote.text: the lifetime value is really high. They're extremely sticky. So rather pay more for better client.
quote.speaker: Chris Conrad

lessons.lesson: A boring, unsexy niche with a physical moat (scarce land) can protect against competition.

quote.text: that land business is why it's difficult, which is actually the moat.
quote.speaker: Chris Conrad

lessons.lesson: Act early and scrappily; learn faster by doing than by reading.

quote.text: you'll learn more in a week by taking action, then reading 300 bucks.
quote.speaker: Chris Conrad

lessons.lesson: Use automation for enforcement (gate lockout on non-payment) to reduce chasing payments.
Let demand data (waitlists, fastest rentals) drive product mix and supply decisions.
Hire hungry, persistent people; Chris hired Eddie because of his relentless persistence.
Maximise income per square foot by adding options like boxes and offices on the same land.

evidence_quality.rationale: Chris is a first-hand operator but numbers are given on camera in a promotional, partly garbled Whisper-tiny transcript; the key financials are not independently verified, the business requires large capital, and the host's challenge ended without a pitch. Claims like 'five hours a week' and '$25k/month' are unverified.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Chris sells a book ('Sell Storage Yards: the Cash Flow Fast Pass') and teaches the model; UpFlip promotes its free business guide, LLC formation service and Niche Finder tool.
